title: Didn't Make It to Milan? Come See This Year's 15 Standout Showings | Great Design
excerpt: Every weekend, QDaily picks a theme and hunts down great design for you.
body:
Every weekend, QDaily picks a theme and hunts down great design for you.

The WeChat official account for "Great Design" is live — search "BestDesign" or "Qthings" to subscribe and follow the new design we turn up every day.

Milan Design Week, as busy and sprawling as ever, is still running. After a week of tracking the coverage, our reaction is simple: too many shows, and too many new pieces to look at without your eyes glazing over.

For the past two weeks our daily Great Design column has kept posting the work unveiled at this year's Salone del Mobile in Milan. Now, for the weekend, we have gathered a batch of the Milan debuts that drew the most praise and the most attention — from brands and designers alike — and put them all in one place. Read through them and you can see some of the new thinking and new directions in furniture design right now.

## Moooi's 2016 New Pieces

The Dutch brand Moooi is a fixture at Milan Design Week. This year its showroom took "Rebellions Harmony" as its theme and reportedly brought together work from 17 designers. One example: founder Marcel Wanders's classic Charleston Chair sofa, turned 90 degrees and stood on end. It leaves the floor entirely, held up instead by a metal axis, so that one armrest becomes the seat while the original seat and back together form the new back — a rebellious touch.

![Marcel Wanders's Charleston Chair sofa turned on end](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140506ncI6u28YGNxCwFtM.jpg-w600)

British designer Paul Cocksedge's marble sofa also takes a twisted, abstract shape rather than a neat symmetrical one, with padding on only a small strip in the middle. It breaks with the usual way of designing a sofa, and reads more as a decorative object.

![Paul Cocksedge's marble sofa](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140506ekUVudxa2KQEmHSR.jpg-w600)

![Another view of Paul Cocksedge's marble sofa](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140506kAXhfP8HuGwItmr5.jpg-w600)

London designer Umut Yamac showed a set of lamps modeled on birds, six in all. The bird shapes have the look of folded paper, set off by brass bases and brass detailing — quite distinctive.

![Umut Yamac's bird lamps](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140507MovB81tSLZp0yFnY.jpg-w600)

![Another of Umut Yamac's bird lamps](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140507OAx4hM7VoB3ntPUa.jpg-w600)

## HAY's 2016 New Pieces

The French duo Ronan and Erwan Bouroullec and the Dutch studio Scholten & Baijings are HAY's star designers. The fence-like furniture collection the Bouroullecs worked on has only just reached stores, and now the pair has collaborated again on a sofa called Can. It has a metal frame and a very square profile; fabric stretched across it supports the back and armrests, with cushions laid on top — simple and unfussy.

![HAY's Can sofa by Ronan and Erwan Bouroullec](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140508o7PqCEymMz1ZUQRF.jpg-w600)

![Another view of the Can sofa](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405087ZXTwsrMy5DjOCgb.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the Can sofa's metal frame](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070214050920zmThSHBY68WEu3.jpg-w600)

Scholten & Baijings brought the 13Eighty chair. Its shape is plain, with fine, evenly spaced holes across the back and the seat — small and simple, and easy for water to drain through.

![Scholten & Baijings's 13Eighty chair for HAY](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140509zkPx09dWnZesfHMm.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the perforated seat of the 13Eighty chair](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140510C9BL2kEv4sb1H5nY.jpg-w600)

There is also a set of wooden chairs called Soft Edge from the Danish studio Iskos-Berlin, made with a double-curved molding technique that gives the wood panels a slight bend for comfort.

![The Soft Edge wooden chair by Iskos-Berlin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405100Qu1vtIeMiN2EwXb.jpg-w600)

What matters most about the first two pieces is that they come apart, which means they can be sold on online furniture sites such as Hem. In a recent interview, founder Rolf Hay talked about designing knockdown furniture to suit the Chinese market and Chinese apartments, on something like IKEA's model — these pieces are an answer to that.

## Wrong London's New Pieces

Wrong London is a lighting brand that grew out of Wrong for HAY not long ago. At Milan Design Week it showed four pieces as the brand's first collection, still working the way it always has — through collaborations with designers and other brands — and the four differ widely in setting and character.

French designer Pierre Charpin made a set of aluminum table lamps with a head that turns; the light adjusts to changes in the light around it, and switches itself off after six hours. Dutch designer Johan van Hengel developed a cone-shaped wooden pendant lamp, its stained and lacquered oak still showing a fine grain — a plain form that holds up to looking at. A collaboration with the Dutch textile brand Vlisco used two of its fabrics as lampshades; Vlisco does a great deal of business in Africa, and the shades carry some of that ethnic patterning. And with Drum Shade the brand made a lamp of marble marked like the surface of the moon.

![Pierre Charpin's aluminum table lamp for Wrong London](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140511XVAseRWM49SmNwrL.jpg-w600)

![Another view of Pierre Charpin's table lamp](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140512i2316Zc5DU9sKy4T.jpg-w600)

![Johan van Hengel's cone-shaped wooden pendant lamp](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140512puq2GHFOWmfh5coB.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the stained and lacquered oak shade](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140512anOtoh10x3IXVPkg.jpg-w600)

![Lampshades made from two Vlisco fabrics](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140513jmcVYQKMZPRIo1de.jpg-w600)

![The marble lamp made with Drum Shade](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140514p3VIStmexl0bBFXR.jpg-w600)

## New Pieces from 2016/

2016/ is a Japanese ceramics brand new to Milan Design Week. It draws on 400 years of pottery in Arita, Japan, but has brought in designers with international reputations — Scholten & Baijings, Stefan Diez, Tomas Alonso — to add playfulness and contemporary design. It is something of an experiment.

Some of the designers work their effects through color and pattern; others break the old shapes, like the half-moon plate from the London studio Tomas Alonso, which even its designers can't say what to do with. Together the pieces show a wider range of form and imagination, and leave the brand itself full of possibility and expectation.

![Ceramics from the Japanese brand 2016/](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140514GsWmA84U7rY953bx.jpg-w600)

![A patterned piece from the 2016/ collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405151Ifp0DO2X8TZCMgu.jpg-w600)

![Tableware from the 2016/ collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405159TLIMGWw6yx4bCF3.jpg-w600)

![Another 2016/ piece](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140515LNv1EFOSd7eyrDJM.jpg-w600)

![Cups from the 2016/ collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405164IeM2FbALkzPOJRf.jpg-w600)

![The half-moon plate designed by Tomas Alonso](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140517BrNw1G4IYtTdhW3a.jpg-w600)

![More pieces from the 2016/ collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140517XEVhdT6qZBl3vrCj.jpg-w600)

## Neri&Hu's 2016 New Pieces

If you were lucky enough to get to this year's Salone del Mobile, your chances of walking into something new from Neri&Hu were probably high. The studio worked with several brands this time and released a good deal of new work.

Take the coat rack it designed for the Swedish furniture brand OFFECCT: a clean, modern form offered as a tribute to plain, everyday multifunctional furniture.

![Neri&Hu's coat rack for OFFECCT](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405189u7vdMsf8GLgE3J2.jpg-w600)

![Another view of the OFFECCT coat rack](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140518Vews6d4SxrWnCtjO.jpg-w600)

Invited back by the Spanish rug brand Nanimarquina, Neri&Hu designed a rug called Jie, the Chinese word for street. It is said to take its cue from the streets of Shanghai: the pattern comes from street textures, and it carries the word for street because the street is what defines a city — the coming and going of people, the noise of a crowded downtown, all woven into this thickly textured rug.

![Neri&Hu's Jie rug for Nanimarquina](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140519tF6wodafp8DjxrRM.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the Jie rug's street-like texture](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140519AZRjE41Hp7Uhq0z6.jpg-w600)

Neri&Hu also designed the Sul and Soo pendant lamp for the well-known Italian lighting brand Viabizzuno. The design and the making are exacting: a slim cord and the bulb hang securely from leather straps and brass hooks, and the light, sheathed in clear glass, throws off a bright shimmer. The lamp first appeared back in March, at the Seoul flagship store of the Korean cosmetics brand Sulwhasoo — a store Neri&Hu also designed, architecture and interiors both.

![The Sul and Soo pendant lamp for Viabizzuno](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140520u5tVQB1eDcTqOxX3.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the leather straps and brass hooks](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140520C53GqYi0VlNOwEsf.jpg-w600)

Invited as well by the Italian furniture brand Driade, Neri&Hu designed the Balance candle holder. A brass ring fixes a candle at one end of a wooden stand, while a metal disc balances the other end and holds small valuables.

![Neri&Hu's Balance candle holder for Driade](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140521G47WERhgi6rQDSbA.jpg-w600)

![Another view of the Balance candle holder](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140522YOyI7ojtAr9V48nP.jpg-w600)

And for the high-end Italian furniture brand Poltrona Frau, Neri&Hu designed the Supporting Ren series of storage pieces, meant to go with the big traditional items — sofas, beds, tables and chairs, cabinets. Set in different corners of a home, they give you somewhere to hang clothes and put personal things.

![A piece from Neri&Hu's Supporting Ren series for Poltrona Frau](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140523pgXIluBRkHa9yVd0.jpg-w600)

## Hermès's 2016-2017 Home Collection

That the French luxury brand Hermès likes to play with furniture is old news. Timed to Milan Design Week, it put out its 2016-2017 Home Collection: sofas, chairs, trays, blankets, screens, magazine baskets and cabinets. There is also a rather striking magnifying glass, a brass cone wrapped in tan calfskin.

![The Hermès magnifying glass, a brass cone wrapped in tan calfskin](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140523wmhpkCABc4a3FyWM.jpg-w600)

The oria d'Hermès chairs are said to follow the shape of the oria chair Rafael Moneo designed for his own house in the early 1960s. The Sellier sofa, by designer Noé Duchaufour-Lawrance, pairs cinnamon-colored flammée printed fabric with tan calfskin.

![A chair from the oria d'Hermès collection](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405246EftuH8MowdXv0aF.jpg-w600)

![Another oria d'Hermès chair](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/201607021405246ihCjRF5clpo3Hek.jpg-w600)

![The Sellier sofa by Noé Duchaufour-Lawrance](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140525L4FIwYrRWV9uz73n.jpg-w600)

## Axor WaterDream bathroom visions

The well-known German bathroom brand Axor invites a group of internationally known designers every year to look into what water means in the spaces people live in, and to make new designs for the bathroom of the future. At this year's Milan Design Week, Axor asked five different teams — David Adjaye, Werner Aisslinger, FRONT, Gamfratesi and Jean-Marie Massaud — to design five very distinctive showerheads, each built on Axor's U-base fitting.

Jean-Marie Massaud's Mimicry, for instance, uses simple geometry rendered in marble so that the water fitting merges into the architecture around it. FRONT's Water Steps is a finely made metal showerhead where water runs from one ledge down to the next, so the streams keep changing.

![Another of the Axor WaterDream showerheads](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140528NmxevWwf4lU3dR0Q.jpg-w600)

## Lollipop by Boris Klimek for Lasvit

Czech designer Boris Klimek made a lollipop-shaped pendant lamp this year for the Czech lighting brand Lasvit, full of childlike play — his usual wry, funny register.

The lamp is said to come from a childhood game: those magic convex glass lenses that warp everything around you when you look through them. It works on exactly that relation between glass and light. Klimek shaped the glass into all kinds of irregular forms and set special bubble structures inside, and with the shifts of color added, they end up looking like clear, glistening lollipops.

![Boris Klimek's Lollipop pendant lamps for Lasvit](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140529lZFEQoGMr8digy3L.jpg-w600)

## Matteo Thun's Latest Collection

Italian architect Matteo Thun used Milan Design Week to launch the first collection of his own furniture brand, all of it handmade: upholstered armchairs, sofas, wooden chairs, and decorative ceramics and glass. Striped vases blown by hand by Venetian craftsmen and clay pots made by Tuscan potters carry a plain, handmade feel, while their colors and shapes are unusually lively and young.

## Patricia Urquiola's New Pieces

Spanish designer Patricia Urquiola became design director of the Italian brand Cassina last year. At this year's Milan Design Week she designed a sofa for the Italian brand Moroso and a storage cabinet for Spazio Pontaccio. The sofa's armrests and back are folded over and buckled to each other with leather straps, which gives it a soft, loose feel; even the corners of the cushions are sewn with leather pads — a design carried all the way through, and its own thing.

![Patricia Urquiola's sofa for Moroso](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140533YK92bDPcoJglNTSk.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the leather straps buckling the back and armrests](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140534OeEdhYDPkgFnR0M9.jpg-w600)

![Another view of the Moroso sofa](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140534pcTueCgMtwSm3EyX.jpg-w600)

![Leather padding sewn into the cushion corners](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140535e5ivpdTBU1JIQZAR.jpg-w600)

She made the storage cabinet with graphic designer Federico Pepe, using the kind of stained glass more often found in buildings or churches. Circles, triangles, squares and other geometric shapes laid out across the cabinet doors give it a modern, decorative style.

![The stained-glass storage cabinet for Spazio Pontaccio](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140535ICNmh8G73qxOHfPB.jpg-w600)

![Detail of the geometric stained-glass doors](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/20160702140536o8PIf7l4jnEMA1rx.jpg-w600)

![Another view of the cabinet](http://img.qdaily.com/uploads/2016070214053746obmyv1T0pLZqwR.jpg-w600)

## Hem's New Furniture Collection

The online furniture brand Hem brought six new pieces this time. They differ in function, use and shape, but because Hem sells online, what it asked of its designers was flat packing and easy shipping.

German designer Karoline Fesser designed two of them, a drum-shaped side table and an all-wood stool. The Stockholm studio Form Us With Love brought a sofa called "Dash to upholster the Koti." The Zig Zag stand comes from the London studio deFORM, made of solid oak and assembled without a single screw. The stool Max Lamb made for the brand comes in a range of colors. Taken together, this is a trim, tidy set with no ornament to spare — pieces that go with almost anything.

## Palladio collection by Claesson Koivisto Rune & Artifort

The table from the Dutch brand Artifort was designed by the Swedish studio Claesson Koivisto Rune, and it is plainly Nordic. It comes in only the two most basic shapes, square or round; the cylindrical iron legs are set in beside the wooden top, sometimes in a different color from it and visible straight from the surface — a small break with the usual detailing, quietly amusing. The tables have no crossbars at all, which keeps them very simple, and tables of different heights and shapes can be pushed together to make a new one.

## Ercol's New Collection

This trim-looking set of furniture comes from the British design brand Ercol, and it suits a home as well as a workplace. The new pieces include a sofa and oak tables and chairs; the shapes are simple, but you can still see elegance and use in the curved armrest structures, the folding round table, and the wooden shelving with cabinets — which also lets the pieces fit more kinds of room. Ercol furniture has never won people over on striking design; it cares about function and industrial production. [Here is the brand's story.](http://www.qdaily.com/articles/582.html)

## A-Chair by Thomas Feichtner

This time Australian product designer Thomas Feichtner has brought the A-Chair, a shape pared to the minimum whose real strength is the making. Feichtner has a group of excellent craftsmen to work with, which is what lets him design this way; the joinery here is as traditional as it gets, and the aim was a chair that uses as little material as possible and still does what a chair has to do.

The A-Chair pulls it off: the angled cut of the back runs into the armrests on both sides in one smooth line, and the lower half makes the exact shape of the letter A. Even when no one is sitting in it, it holds its own at home as a good-looking piece of craft.

## Little Big Chair by Big-Game & Magis

Children's furniture was another hot topic this year — we wrote earlier about a line of plastic children's furniture from Kartell. The Swiss studio Big-Game designed a chair for the Italian brand Magis aimed at young children, ages two to six. The seat, plastic on wooden legs, slides up and down to adjust the height, so it works across several ages; it looks simple but is very practical. The design team says the chair is sturdy and hard-wearing enough for an adult to stand right on it.
